group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 61-year-old man was brought to the emergency department by ambulance in early autumn after two days of progressively worsening shortness of breath, a new cough productive of scant rust-colored sputum, and pleuritic discomfort along the lower left rib cage that awakened him from sleep the night before. According to his wife, he had spent the previous afternoon seated in a recliner because walking from the living room to the kitchen left him winded, whereas he normally climbs the stairs of their split-level home without pausing. His past history is notable for a small left parietal lacunar infarct six years ago that required inpatient rehabilitation for mild expressive aphasia—now fully resolved—and chronic systolic ventricular dysfunction attributed to ischemic cardiomyopathy diagnosed four years earlier after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction; the most recent office echocardiogram three months earlier documented an ejection fraction of 30 % with mild functional mitral regurgitation. Outpatient laboratory panels have consistently shown a creatinine around 0.9 mg/dL, and he has never needed nephrology follow-up or dialysis, nor has he been told he has chronic kidney disease. He also has no known history of chronic liver disease, and prior hepatic function testing has been normal. He takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 24-26 mg twice daily, low-dose furosemide, and aspirin 81 mg; no diuretic dose had been skipped in the week preceding presentation, and he denies use of any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents or over-the-counter cold remedies. He quit cigarettes twenty years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of wine with dinner on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. There has been no recent travel, no exposure to ill contacts, and no prior stays in long-term care facilities; he and his wife prepare their own meals and manage their household independently. On arrival he was seated upright on the gurney, conversant, making eye contact, and answering questions appropriately without confusion or slurred speech. Triage vital signs recorded before any antipyretics, bronchodilators, diuretics, vasodilators, antibiotics, intravenous fluids, or supplemental oxygen showed an oral temperature of 37.3 °C, heart rate 91 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 37 breaths per minute with shallow rapid excursions and mild use of accessory neck muscles, automated blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg confirmed by manual sphygmomanometry, and a room-air pulse oximetry reading that fluctuated between 89 % and 91 % while he sat still. His skin was warm and pink without diaphoresis; mucous membranes were moist. Jugular venous pulsation was visible 6 cm above the sternal angle when the head of bed was raised to 45°, similar to prior clinic examinations. Cardiac auscultation revealed a regular rhythm with a soft S3 consistent with chronic ventricular dysfunction but no appreciable murmurs or rubs. Lung examination disclosed markedly decreased breath sounds with dullness to percussion at the left posterior costophrenic angle, crackles extending to the inferior half of the left lung field, and scattered coarse crackles over the right lower lobe; no wheezes were appreciated. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, and nontender; the liver edge was not palpable. Extremities were warm with 1+ pitting edema at both ankles, unchanged from baseline per patient report, and capillary refill was <2 seconds. Neurologic screening demonstrated intact cranial nerves, fluent speech, 5/5 strength throughout, and normal rapid alternating movements, matching his outpatient neurologic examination. A bedside finger-stick glucose measured 114 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas obtained on room air within ten minutes of arrival revealed pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, PaO₂ 76 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 23 mEq/L. Laboratory studies drawn simultaneously and processed within twenty minutes showed sodium 127 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L on the chemistry panel, blood urea nitrogen 13 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and hematocrit 29 % with hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume was 84 fL and iron studies from a clinic visit two weeks earlier had suggested chronic disease anemia. White blood cell count returned at 13.2 × 10⁹/L with 86 % segmented neutrophils, platelet count 210 × 10⁹/L, and high-sensitivity troponin I was below detection threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy depicted a dense consolidation occupying the lingular segment of the left upper lobe with air bronchograms and blunting of the adjacent costophrenic angle by a curvilinear meniscus of fluid; the cardiac silhouette was mildly enlarged but unchanged from films three months prior, and pulmonary vasculature was not congested. Point-of-care thoracic ultrasonography confirmed an anechoic stripe approximately 9 mm thick above the left hemidiaphragm consistent with a small free-flowing effusion. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 90 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T changes identical to old tracings and Q-waves in V1–V3 from his prior infarct. Two sets of blood cultures, a sputum Gram stain, and respiratory viral PCR panel were obtained before any antimicrobial agents. At the close of the initial evaluation he remained seated upright on room air, had received no medications or intravenous fluids aside from the 5 mL heparinized saline flush used for arterial sampling, and continued to engage appropriately with staff while awaiting disposition.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age → 61. Lives at home, so no nursing-home points → 0.
- Comorbidities: chronic systolic heart failure (EF 30%) → 10; cerebrovascular disease (prior lacunar infarct, even though deficits resolved) → 10. No documented malignancy, liver disease, or renal disease → 0.
- Examination: respiratory rate 37/min (≥30) → 20. Mentation normal, systolic BP 126 mm Hg (not <90), temperature 37.3 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 91/min (<125) → 0 each.
- Labs: sodium 127 mEq/L (<130) → 20; hematocrit 29% (<30%) → 10. Arterial pH 7.50 (not <7.35), BUN 13 mg/dL (<30), and glucose 114 mg/dL (<250) → 0 each. Using the measured room-air PaO₂ of 76 mm Hg, the <60 mm Hg criterion is not met → 0.
- Imaging: confirmed pleural effusion → 10.
Total = 61 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 10 + 10 = 141.
Final answer: 141
